# SK3062 — `this` escapes before the constructor finishes

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A constructor stores `this` in another type's static state, hands it to an object reached through a static field, subscribes it to a static event, or captures it in a delegate it starts on another thread.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S3366 |

## Why

A constructor's body runs before the derived constructors, before the readonly fields are visible to other threads under a weak memory model, and before anything the caller was going to do with the finished object. Publishing `this` from inside it hands somebody a reference to an object that is not there yet. ⚠ **The three destinations here are the ones where the second reader is not under the constructor's control**: static state outlives every instance, and a thread the constructor starts races the rest of the constructor by construction. On ARM64 the second thread can legally observe a field before its initializer, which is the failure that never reproduces on the developer's x64 machine.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Worker {
    readonly int[] buffer;

    public Worker(int size) {
        Task.Run(() => Drain());     // races the line below
        buffer = new int[size];
    }

    void Drain() { /* buffer may still be null here */ }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Worker {
    readonly int[] buffer;

    Worker(int size) => buffer = new int[size];

    public static Worker Start(int size) {
        var worker = new Worker(size);
        Task.Run(worker.Drain);

        return worker;
    }

    void Drain() { }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Fixless.** Every repair — a factory that constructs and then publishes, a separate `Start`, a deferred subscription — moves code out of the constructor into a place the rule cannot choose, because which caller becomes responsible for the second step is a design decision the constructor does not contain. ⚠ **What the rule refuses to report is the rule.** `button.Click += OnClick;` in a constructor is the overwhelmingly common *legitimate* shape — nearly every UI type ever written contains it — and a rule that reports it is worse than no rule, because it would be dismissed wholesale and take the four real shapes with it. So only publication whose **second reader is outside the constructor's control** is reported: process-wide static state, or a thread the constructor itself starts. Subscribing to an instance event on a field, a local, a parameter or `this` is declined, and there is a fixture for each of those four rather than one standing for all of them. ⚠ **`this` passed to a static *method* is not publication and is not reported.** `Console.WriteLine(this)`, `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(this)` and a validation helper all read their argument and keep nothing; admitting them would bury the rule. Only a call whose *receiver* is a static field or property counts, because that is the object that outlives the constructor. ⚠ **Shape A stops at the constructor's own type, and the boundary is `SK2134`.** `current = this;` writing this type's own static field is the canonical shape of `instance-write-to-static` and is already reported there; two findings on one line is a double-report, and a reader who has to choose which of two to act on acts on neither. ⚠ **A `Thread` must be created *and* started inside the same constructor.** `new Thread(Work)` stored in a field and started later is not a race and is declined. A delegate that closes over only locals, parameters and statics does not reach `this` and is declined too. ⚠ **And shape D declines a `sealed` type that starts the thread as its last act, which is a gate the reference tree bought.** The first draft reported Vixen's `VideoPlayer` and that finding was *wrong*: `Thread.Start`, `Task.Run` and `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem` all publish a memory barrier, so everything the constructor wrote before them is visible to the new thread, and a sealed type has no derived constructor left to run — nothing changes after the publication, so nothing races. The rule now requires something that still changes afterwards: a statement following the start at any enclosing level, or a type that is not sealed. ⚠ **Shapes A, B and C deliberately do not share that gate.** Storing a reference in static state is not a barrier and buys no ordering, and the defect there is that the object is reachable at all before the caller has the reference to undo it — not that it is unfinished. ⚠ **The framework types are resolved from the compilation, never matched on the written name.** `Thread` and `Task` are both plausible names for somebody's own type, and a finding on one of those sends a reader to threading code that does not exist.
